items_missed: Special considerations never asked. No question about anything heavy, fragile, antique or awkward — on a move that includes a king-size headboard, a tall wooden dresser, a wooden bench and a dining table, hauled a hundred feet down a storage-facility hallway and then up a flight of stairs into a two-story townhome. He had moved this customer before and used that history to size the job, but he never asked what is in the load this time that needs care.

Packing needs never asked. The customer volunteered 'No, I'll do all of those' about boxes at the house, and that closed the topic — nobody asked whether she wants packing service at the storage unit or the apartment.

Moving stressors never asked — no 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?' This is a next-day, three-stop, move-out-of-a-boyfriend's-house situation and the question was never put.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. A repeat customer, a king headboard, a tall dresser, and a hundred-foot storage hallway, and she never heard that the move carries up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned — on a next-day move, where knowing who is arriving at your door tomorrow morning is worth more than usual.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, and this is the single most costly omission on the call. Arrival time was the entire back half of the conversation: she asked 'Do you have anything a little bit later than that by any chance?', they negotiated 8:30 to 10/10:30, she asked twice to confirm the window, and he explained the latest possible start. At no point did anyone say 'and if we miss that window, we start discounting your bill immediately.' That is the differentiator handed to him on a plate.

Estimate built by addition rather than by build-up, and he said so: 'that was just for the storage unit portion and that took about two and a half hours. So, typically for, I mean, for the starting spot for just the living room dining room items, you know, I would maybe add an hour or two on top of that to, to get this done just to be safe.' 'Add an hour or two... just to be safe' is a guess with a cushion on it, and the spread between the two ends of that guess is $206.

Disassembly and reassembly never factored into the hours. A king headboard, a bed frame, a wooden dining table and two nightstands are all teardown-and-rebuild items, and the time they consume was never named — the tools being included was mentioned in the pricing block, but not the clock impact.

No deposit required never mentioned. It came closest when she hesitated on the time — 'Can I call you back to confirm?' — which is a commitment-risk moment, and the answer he reached for was truck scarcity rather than 'there's no deposit, so locking it costs you nothing.' Scarcity worked here, but no-deposit is the stronger and more repeatable line.

No 'reply with any corrections' on the confirmation email. He said 'I'll send over the confirmation email let you know that I have you on the schedule for tomorrow. And then if you need to change the time at all, just call us or email us' — that invites a time change, not a verification of the details. On a three-stop move being locked in overnight, with a storage address captured by ear ('25623 roof no drive'), asking her to read it back is the cheapest error-catch available.
BOLDED key details at the top of the email never mentioned.

Office hours never given. He did give the callback number when she asked for it — '817-786-6118 should be the number I called you from' — but nobody said when someone will be there to answer it, on a move happening the next morning.
Effective insurance explanation missed entirely — no No Worries, no 60¢/lb baseline, nothing.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. This is the second-best Save Your Ass setup in the week's sample and it got nothing. The customer said 'No, I'll do all of those' about the boxes, meaning she is already in prep mode and receptive; the storage unit is a hundred-foot hallway walk; there are 'maybe like one or two small ones' in boxes there; and the move is tomorrow, so the advice would have been acted on within hours.
top_strength: Grant runs the cleanest call structure in this week's sample and closes like someone who has done it a thousand times. The agenda landed with a confirmation attached — 'Let me walk you through how our pricing is gonna work and then I'll go over your quote specifically for you. You don't need to write anything down or take any notes. All of this information is going to be sent to the email address that you put on the profile. Does that work for you?' — and the 'you don't need to write anything down' line is a genuinely good touch that lowers the customer's cognitive load before a wall of numbers. The pricing block that followed is the most complete in the batch: the rate framed correctly per mover per hour and then totaled ('$103 per hour per mover on Saturdays. For this, I would just send you a two man team. So that would be $206 an hour'), a full inclusions list, and a fee denial that names the specific fees a customer would fear ('there's no travel fees for us to come out and service you. There's no heavy item fees, like I said, no hidden fees of any type'). He closed it with a check — 'any questions about any of that info so far' — and checked again after the estimate. The close itself is the standout. He asked for the booking directly — 'if you like what you've heard we do have a morning arrival time available for tomorrow, it would be an 8:30 AM arrival time. Do you want to go ahead and get that set up?' — and when she hesitated with 'Can I call you back to confirm?', he did not stall or let it drift. He took control and de-risked it in the same breath: 'we only have one truck available tomorrow and I just don't want you to lose that spot. So I'm gonna put you down for 10-10:30 and I'll send you a confirmation email but if you need to change the time tomorrow, just email us or call us and let us know.' Real scarcity, no pressure, an escape hatch offered before she asked for one, and he even gave her the outer bound so she could plan ('I think the latest we'd be able to start this would be 12-12:30'). She went from 'can I call you back' to booked in under thirty seconds. Then, unprompted and with nothing to gain, he handed her money back: 'just to, real quick while I have you for those moving pads it looks like we charged you for eleven of them at $12 a piece. So once we get those back, you'll get a refund of $132 at the end of it.' That is a rep reading the customer's own file for her benefit, and her reaction — 'Okay, awesome' — is why she called Einstein a second time.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Grant's three biggest misses are all in the same ten seconds of script, and he already had the perfect opening for each. The On-Time Guarantee belonged in the arrival-time negotiation — she asked about the window three times, and 'and just so you know, if we miss that 10 to 10:30 window, we start discounting your bill immediately' would have turned her most anxious topic into a reason to trust the booking. No Worries Damage Coverage belonged in the estimate block — she has a king headboard, a tall wooden dresser and a wooden bench going a hundred feet down a hallway and up a flight of stairs. Meet Your Mover belonged in the confirmation-email moment — on a next-day move, 'you'll also get an email with a photo of the mover coming to you' is reassurance delivered exactly when it is needed. Those three cost roughly twenty seconds and are worth six points of pricing section plus three differentiator flags Einstein is hitting almost nowhere company-wide. Second priority: the Save Your Ass speech is a flat zero and this call was built for it. She is doing her own boxes, the move is tomorrow morning, the storage unit is a hundred-foot walk, and she has 'maybe like one or two small ones' in boxes sitting in that unit. 'One thing that'll save you real money tomorrow, Gabby — anything small you can move yourself, do it tonight. Those one or two boxes at the storage unit, the patio stuff, anything loose. Every trip down that hundred-foot hallway they don't have to make is time off your clock. Does that make sense?' That is the difference between a four-hour move and a four-and-a-half-hour move, on a bill she is paying tomorrow. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: the quote was built by taking a known actual (2.5 hours for the storage portion alone, from her own prior move) and then adding 'an hour or two on top of that to, to get this done just to be safe.' The added scope is real — three stops instead of one, a second-floor townhome with stairs, a living room and dining set that were not in the previous job — so the direction is right. But 'just to be safe' is exactly the padding language driving the 46% accuracy number, and the one-hour spread he left himself is $206 of the customer's money. The better version prices each new piece out loud: 'the storage portion was two and a half last time, the living and dining pickup is another forty-five minutes or so, and the stairs at the townhome add maybe thirty on the unload — so I'm landing at four to four and a half.' Same range, built instead of cushioned, and the customer can follow the logic. Worth pulling the actual against this one when it closes, since the prior-move baseline makes it unusually easy to measure. Third, add the correction ask to the confirmation email — 'give it a quick read and reply if anything's off' — because this call captured a storage address by ear ('25623 roof no drive'), on a move happening in under sixteen hours, with three stops to get right.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and unhurried in a way the customer visibly relaxed into — 'You're fine. You take your time' when she was hunting for the storage unit size, her name used four times including in the farewell, a genuine collaborative check ('I'm gonna say like a hundred feet, you think that's fair'), and the unprompted $132 pad refund that produced the only spontaneous 'Okay, awesome' on the call; short of a 5 only because there is no humor or rapport moment and the language runs on a narrow set of stock affirmations ('Gotcha,' 'Alrighty,' 'good deal').
audio_review_reason: The transcript has him introducing himself as 'Hey, Gabby, this is Brent with Einstein Moving Company' on a call to a repeat customer whose file he is reading. That is either a transcription artifact on 'Grant' or an actual self-introduction error, and the two have completely different coaching implications — one is nothing, the other is a correctable opener mistake on a customer relationship Einstein has already earned once. Audio is needed to settle which, and the same pass can confirm the arrival-window exchange, which reads as slightly tangled in the transcript ('so if with the morning time so if I, if we said 10:00 AM it'd be 10-10:30 arrival time').
